# Technical Building Blocks



Building reliable AI-native design systems requires a rigorous technical substrate. Connecting language models to hardware code generators without physical grounding produces brittle or unviable silicon. In Part II, we define the four modular technical building blocks that every AI-native design system needs (@tbl-part2-roadmap): machine-usable hardware representations, method selection across learned and conventional approaches, tool-connected execution environments, and verification feedback.

These four pillars address the core tension in constructing AI-native design systems: *Machine Usability versus Physical Ground Truth*. Learned surrogate models and fast proxy estimators accelerate search by orders of magnitude, but they systematically exploit simulator blind spots and unmodeled physical constraints (the *Optimizer's Curse*) unless anchored to deterministic tool wrappers and qualification rules. We classify the structural representations that make hardware design state machine-usable, connect learned methods to cycle-accurate simulators and physical signoff tools, and construct the verification feedback loops that qualify results before admitting them into the project record.


::: {.callout-part}
1. How do we maintain machine-usable state alignment between abstract system models and physical silicon constraints?
2. What qualification rules prevent unverified candidate proposals from corrupting subsequent design search steps?
:::
